v.rationale: All three suites pass, and I found no real bugs. Each implementation locks the coupon row with lockForUpdate inside a transaction before it checks for an existing redemption or the cap. This serialises requests across MySQL servers, and a unique(coupon_id,user_id) index backs it up. Each one dispatches the event only after commit and only for the request that created the redemption. My probes passed on all three: a repeat request shows the current count after other users redeem, max_redemptions=0 gives a 409 with a message, an existing redeemer on an exhausted coupon gets 200, and the listener runs after commit. The ranking therefore comes down to idioms. impl-1 keeps the side effect inside the domain method, so creation and event can't be separated, and it has the thinnest controller. It loses a little for copying redeemed_count back onto the bound model and for using null to mean 'exhausted'. impl-2 is about equally clean: a renderable domain exception, firstOrNew/setRelation and transaction retries. But it moves the event dispatch into the controller, so other callers of redeemFor could skip it, and its tests carry some unneeded setup. impl-3 is correct but puts all the logic in a fat controller. It also skips route model binding, returns a tuple, uses abort() as control flow and makes the counter mass-assignable.
